questions.ask: What entity does this denote: the transport circuit itself, a binding/reference from an IP service to that circuit, or something else? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Is this a physical transport demarcation/hand-off, a logical service endpoint, or both? Please give a gloss, example, and relations, including its layer and endpoint identity.
Does this denote committed end-to-end client payload rate, physical bearer line rate, or an IP-service bandwidth attribute? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Does this denote measured one-way propagation delay of the transport circuit, or an IP-service SLA metric? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Does this denote physical transport path protection against fiber/bearer failure, or logical service resilience? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
What dimensions determine this service class? In particular, is it a transport protection/restoration grade or an IP-service commercial/QoS class? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Please give this concept's gloss, example, and relations, especially whether it is client/service encapsulation or transport-internal framing.
Please give this concept's gloss, example, and relations, including how it uses an underlay and connects to attachments.

answers.gloss: The transport circuit itself insofar as an IP service is bound to and rides it; it is owned by the transport domain and referenced/consumed by the service domain, not a separate physical bearer.
answers.example: IP service SVC-42 rides transport underlay circuit U-7.
answers.relations: It carries c.service; conversely c.service rides it. Its identity is the transport circuit's identity, although represented here as the service's underlay binding/reference.

answers.gloss: A logical IP-service endpoint where the service attaches to a customer site/router. It is not, by definition, the physical transport demarcation or hand-off, though deployment may colocate them.
answers.example: att-NY-SVC42 is the New York logical attachment of SVC-42 to the customer router.
answers.relations: It is of c.service and bears c.vlan. Its endpoint identity is service-specific and belongs to the customer-facing IP/Ethernet service layer.

answers.gloss: The committed information rate guaranteed for customer traffic as an IP-service bandwidth attribute, not the physical bearer line rate.
answers.example: SVC-42 has a CIR of 5 Gbit/s even if its transport bearer has a higher line rate.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of c.service and specifies committed client-traffic capacity.

answers.gloss: An IP-service SLA latency commitment expressed as a named tier, rather than the raw measured propagation delay of a transport circuit.
answers.example: SVC-42 uses tier T2, committing to latency of at most 8 ms.
answers.relations: It is an SLA attribute of c.service; transport delay may support the commitment but is not this concept's identity.

answers.gloss: The logical service-resilience requirement that service connectivity survive failure in its transport path. It states the service outcome, not a particular physical protection mechanism.
answers.example: SVC-42 must remain connected after one underlay-path failure.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of c.service and constrains how its underlay connectivity must be engineered.

answers.gloss: The IP class of service applied by routers, determining scheduling and drop priority; it is not a transport protection or restoration grade.
answers.example: Gold traffic for SVC-42 enters a low-latency queue, while silver and bronze receive different treatment.
answers.relations: It is a QoS/class attribute of c.service and governs packet treatment in the IP layer.

answers.gloss: The customer VLAN tag that identifies service traffic on an attachment; it is client/service Ethernet encapsulation, not transport-internal framing.
answers.example: C-VLAN 100 identifies SVC-42 traffic at its New York attachment.
answers.relations: It is carried on c.attachment and belongs to the customer-facing IP/Ethernet service layer.

answers.gloss: The end-to-end IP/VPN service delivered to the customer. It rides a transport underlay but remains a distinct higher-layer entity that the transport domain does not identify as the service.
answers.example: SVC-42 is a point-to-point IP service joining New York and Frankfurt over transport circuit U-7.
answers.relations: It rides c.underlay and attaches at one or more c.attachment endpoints; its CIR, latency tier, resilience requirement, and IP QoS class are represented by c.rate, c.latency, c.protection, and c.grade.

questions.ask: Does this denote the transport circuit itself, and can a higher-layer IP service bind to it as an underlay? Please give gloss, example, endpoint identity, capacity, and relations to bearers and hand-offs.
Is this a physical transport demarcation, a logical circuit endpoint, or a higher-layer service attachment? Please give gloss, example, layer, endpoint identity, and relations.
Is this physical circuit/bearer line capacity, committed payload capacity, or another rate? Please give gloss, example, and relations.
Is this raw/measured transport-circuit delay or a named end-customer service SLA commitment? Please give gloss, representation, example, and relations.
Does this denote a transport protection mechanism/path property or an outcome-level logical service resilience requirement? Please give gloss, example, and relations.
Which dimensions determine this transport grade—such as protection/restoration behavior, physical quality, or packet scheduling/drop priority? Please give gloss, example, and relations.
What transport entity does bearer denote, and how does it differ from m.circuit? Please give gloss, example, layer, capacity, connectivity, and relations.

answers.gloss: The provisioned end-to-end transport circuit itself. A higher-layer IP service may bind to and ride it as its underlay, but the circuit remains a transport-domain entity distinct from that service.
answers.example: CIR-7 connects the New York and Frankfurt transport hand-offs and may carry IP service SVC-42.
answers.relations: It presents at physical m.handoff endpoints and is carried on physical optical m.bearer resources. Its endpoint identity is the pair of transport hand-offs; its capacity is the committed client payload rate represented by m.rate, not the bearer wavelength's line rate.

answers.gloss: The physical transport demarcation where a circuit presents to client equipment; it is not a service-specific logical IP attachment.
answers.example: ho-NY-CIR7 is the physical port where CIR-7 meets the customer router in New York.
answers.relations: It is a transport-layer endpoint on m.circuit. Its identity belongs to the circuit/physical demarcation and can be colocated with, but is not identical to, a higher-layer service attachment.

answers.gloss: The committed client payload capacity guaranteed end to end by a transport circuit, rather than the optical bearer's physical line rate.
answers.example: CIR-7 guarantees 5 Gbit/s of client payload even if its carrying wavelength operates at a higher line rate.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of m.circuit and describes circuit capacity. It is not an attribute of a distinct higher-layer IP service.

answers.gloss: The raw measured one-way propagation delay of a transport circuit, represented numerically in units such as milliseconds; it is not a named end-customer SLA tier.
answers.example: CIR-7's primary path has a measured one-way delay of 7.2 ms.
answers.relations: It is a path-length-dependent attribute of m.circuit. A higher-layer service may use this measurement to support an SLA, but the SLA commitment is a different concept.

answers.gloss: A transport protection mechanism/property that switches a circuit to a diverse transport path after fiber, bearer, or path failure.
answers.example: CIR-7 uses 1+1 path protection so a primary fiber cut triggers use of the diverse path.
answers.relations: It is an attribute of m.circuit and concerns concrete physical transport-path protection, rather than merely specifying a higher-layer service-connectivity outcome.

answers.gloss: The transport quality grade of a circuit, determined by its physical protection and restoration class, not by packet scheduling or drop priority.
answers.example: CIR-7 is platinum grade because it is dual-path protected; other grades include gold and best-effort.
answers.relations: It classifies m.circuit according to transport protection/restoration behavior and has no IP QoS queueing semantics.

answers.gloss: A physical optical transport resource—typically a wavelength on fiber—on which one or more circuits are carried. It is lower-layer and transport-internal, unlike the provisioned client-facing circuit.
answers.example: The 193.1 THz wavelength on the NY–FRA span carries CIR-7.
answers.relations: It carries m.circuit. Its connectivity follows optical fiber spans, and its physical line capacity may exceed a carried circuit's committed m.rate; it has no client-facing service endpoint identity.

proposals.rationale: B states that c.underlay has the transport circuit's own identity and is the transport-domain circuit consumed by a higher-layer service, not a separate bearer. That denotes m.circuit viewed through the service's underlay reference.

ratifications.reason: Both denote the same provisioned transport-domain circuit, with transport endpoint identity, that the higher-layer IP service references and rides as its underlay. c.underlay is not a separate bearer or merely an abstract binding object.
